headline: Six levels cost next-yak nothing over three, because the whole chain compiles to one `__yak_button` holding six classes in a single string, while every lane that merges at render pays six times.

microbench.why: Five wrappers over a base button, each adding one declaration. `next-yak` compiles all six levels to `__yak_button("yRGSbEH yRGSbEH1 … yRGSbEH5")`, one component and one class string, and renders at 1.48M renders/s, the same figure it posts at depth three. `next-yak-nofold` at 1.18M keeps all six wrappers and shows exactly what the fold removes. Hand-written `vanilla` at 919,000 now sits below both yak lanes, because six React functions and six string joins are not free even with no library involved. `next-yak-css` at 600,000 runs `mergeCssProp` six times, and `panda` at 310,000 re-resolves six style objects per instance.

autocannon.why: `next-yak` at 1,206 req/s barely moves from its depth-three figure while `vanilla` falls to 840 and `panda` to 191. Depth under load is where the compile-time and render-time strategies separate most plainly.

attribution.why: `next-yak` totals 0.808 ms, indistinguishable from the 0.797 ms it spends at depth three, with 0.402 ms of lib self-time inside the single folded wrapper. `vanilla` needs 1.24 ms, 0.395 ms of it component self-time spread over six functions and 0.844 ms in React itself. `next-yak-css` reaches 2.84 ms and `goober` 4.85 ms, both paying once per level.

hydrate.why: Hydration on the compose cases is bimodal, with modes near 45 ms and 90 ms that swap between batteries, so the ordering inside the leading group is noise rather than mechanism. `vanilla` at 49.5 ms and `bamboo` at 49.6 ms hold the fast mode; `next-yak` reads 88.1 ms here against 46.6 ms previously. `styled-components` at 96.2 ms and `goober` at 107 ms sit high in both.

inp.why: Eight lanes answer one click between 7.0 ms and 8.0 ms. `goober` at 23.1 ms, `panda` at 14.8 ms and `emotion` at 11.2 ms are the exceptions, all re-deriving the full six-level chain on the component that was clicked.

mount.why: `next-yak` leads at 71.4 ms in a band running to 89.4 ms for twelve lanes. Six levels add render work, and mount is dominated by parse and layout, so the ordering compresses against what the microbench shows.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane, 0.129 ms to 0.188 ms. Six levels of composition still produce one element and the same matching work.

payload.why: Depth is nearly free on the wire for the compile-time lanes: `next-yak` ships 4,112 gz B against 3,958 B at depth three, the difference being three more small rules. `vanilla` holds the floor at 3,075 B. The runtime lanes are unchanged from depth one, because what fills their payload is the library rather than the chain.

nsweep.why: `next-yak` at 2.84 ms at the largest size is close to its depth-three figure, while `next-yak-nofold` needs 3.22 ms and `vanilla` 4.22 ms. Per-level work sets the slope, and a folded chain has no per-level work to set one with.

crossCase: The deep end of the trio, with the Examples `compose-1` and `compose-3`. `next-yak` costs 2.24M, 1.40M and 1.48M renders/s across the three depths, so everything after the first wrapper is free and the chain concatenates into one component whatever its depth. Every other lane pays per level, most steeply `panda` at 1.12M, 540,000 and 310,000.
